01

Tangent line from the derivative

Derivative and tangent lines
Source p.1
Lecture Differentiation slides 2–4Ref sheet A1 · Tangents and ratesRelated Tutorial 3, 5
Method Differentiate → slope at point → point–slope equation.
1
Find the equation of the tangent line to the parabola \(y=2x-3x^2\) at the point \((1,-1)\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(y=-4x+3\)
  1. \(f'(x)=2-6x\): use the power rule.
  2. \(f'(1)=2-6=-4\): tangent gradient.
  3. \(y+1=-4(x-1)\); expand to obtain the equation.
02

Read a derivative from a known tangent

Derivative as slope
Source p.1
Lecture Differentiation slides 2–6Ref sheet A1 · Tangents and ratesRelated Tutorial 3, 9
Method At the specified x, the line height is f(x), and its slope is f′(x).
2
The tangent line to \(y=f(x)\) at \(x=2\) is \(y=4x-5\). Find \(f(2)\) and \(f'(2)\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f(2)=3,\quad f'(2)=4\)
  1. \(f(2)=4(2)-5=3\) because the tangent touches the curve.
  2. \(f\prime(2)=4\) because 4 is the line gradient.
03

Tangent from point and slope

Point–slope form
Source p.1
Lecture Differentiation slides 2–4Ref sheet A1 · Tangents and ratesRelated Tutorial 1, 2
Method Use y−y₀ = m(x−x₀).
3
Find the tangent line at \(x=4\) when \(f(4)=2\) and \(f'(4)=3\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(y=3x-10\)
  1. \(y-2=3(x-4)\); derivative is slope and given function value fixes the point.
  2. \(y=3x-10\).
04

Normal line through a known point

Tangent/normal perpendicularity
Source p.1
Lecture Differentiation slides 2–4, 10–13Ref sheet A1 · Tangents and normalsRelated Tutorial 5
Method Normal gradient is negative reciprocal of nonzero tangent gradient.
4
Find the normal to \(y=x\sqrt x\) at \((1,1)\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(y-1=-\tfrac23(x-1)\)
  1. \(y=x^{3/2}\Rightarrow y\prime=\tfrac32\sqrt x\).
  2. \(m_t=\tfrac32\) at x=1; \(m_n=-1/m_t=-\tfrac23\).
  3. \(y-1=-\tfrac23(x-1)\).
05

Normal parallel to a given line

Parallel slopes
Source p.1
Lecture Differentiation slides 2–4, 10–13Ref sheet A1 · Tangents and normalsRelated Tutorial 4, 9
Method Get target slope → tangent negative reciprocal → solve x → substitute point.
5
Find the normal to \(y=\sqrt x\) parallel to \(2x+y=1\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(y=-2x+3\)
  1. \(2x+y=1\Rightarrow y=-2x+1\) has slope −2.
  2. \(m_t=\tfrac12\) because the normal is perpendicular.
  3. \(y'=1/(2\sqrt x)=\tfrac12\Rightarrow x=1,\;y=1\).
  4. \(y-1=-2(x-1)\Rightarrow y=-2x+3\).
06

Average versus instantaneous cost

Rates of change
Source p.1
Lecture Differentiation slides 4–6Ref sheet A1 · Rate of changeRelated Tutorial 1, 7
Method Average uses a difference quotient; instantaneous uses derivative at the specified x.
6a
The cost is \(C(x)=5000+10x+0.05x^2\). Find average rate when production changes from 100 to 105 units.
Show worked solution+
Result \(20.25\ \text{dollars/unit}\)
  1. \(\bar r=[C(105)-C(100)]/(105-100)\).
  2. \(\bar r=10+0.05(105+100)=20.25\).
  3. A cost rate has units dollars per additional unit.
6b
For \(C(x)=5000+10x+0.05x^2\), find instantaneous rate at \(x=100\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(20\ \text{dollars/unit}\)
  1. \(C'(x)=10+0.1x\).
  2. \(C'(100)=10+0.1(100)=20\); this is marginal cost at x=100.
07

Derivative from first principles

First derivative formula
Source p.1
Lecture Differentiation slides 3–8Ref sheet A1 · First principlesRelated Tutorial 10c, 10l
Method Substitute x+h, subtract, rationalize/factor h, then take h→0.
7
For \(f(x)=\sqrt x,\ x\ge0\), find the derivative using the first derivative formula.
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=\tfrac1{2\sqrt x}\quad(x>0)\)
  1. \(f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}(\sqrt{x+h}-\sqrt x)/h\).
  2. \((\sqrt{x+h}-\sqrt x)/h=1/(\sqrt{x+h}+\sqrt x)\) by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate.
  3. \(h\to0\Rightarrow f\prime(x)=1/(2\sqrt x)\) for x>0.
  4. At x=0, the right-hand quotient tends to +∞, so there is no finite derivative.
08

Horizontal tangents

Stationary points
Source p.1
Lecture Differentiation slides 6, 18–21Ref sheet A5 · ExtremaRelated Tutorial 15, 22
Method Horizontal tangent means f′(x)=0, then compute every y-coordinate.
8
Find points on \(y=x^4-6x^2+4\) with horizontal tangent.
Show worked solution+
Result \((0,4),\ (\sqrt3,-5),\ (-\sqrt3,-5)\)
  1. \(y'=4x^3-12x=4x(x^2-3)\).
  2. \(y'=0\Rightarrow x=0,\ \pm\sqrt3\).
  3. \(y(0)=4,\quad y(\pm\sqrt3)=9-18+4=-5\).
09

Tangent parallel to a specified line

Derivative matching a gradient
Source p.1
Lecture Differentiation slides 6, 10–13Ref sheet A1 · Tangents and normalsRelated Tutorial 5, 8
Method For parallel lines equate derivative to the required slope.
9
Find the point on \(y=e^x\) where tangent is parallel to \(y=3x\).
Show worked solution+
Result \((\ln 3,3)\)
  1. \(y'=e^x\) and target slope is 3.
  2. \(e^x=3\Rightarrow x=\ln3\).
  3. \(y=e^{\ln3}=3\).
10

Differentiate every listed function

Power/product/chain/log/inverse trig
Source p.1
Lecture Differentiation slides 10–17Ref sheet A2–A4 · Derivative rulesRelated Tutorial 7, 11, 25
Method Identify outer/inner, then apply chain, product, quotient, or log rule.
10a
Differentiate \(f(x)=e^{35},\ x\in\mathbb R\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=0\)
  1. e^{35} is independent of x: the derivative of any constant is zero.
10b
Differentiate \(f(x)=3^{100},\ x\in\mathbb R\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=0\)
  1. The base and exponent are both constants, so the expression is constant.
10c
Differentiate \(y(x)=\frac{\sqrt x+x}{x^2},\ x>0\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(y\prime=-\frac3{2x^{5/2}}-\frac1{x^2}\)
  1. \(y=x^{-3/2}+x^{-1}\) by dividing both numerator terms by x².
  2. \(y\prime=-\tfrac32x^{-5/2}-x^{-2}\) by the power rule.
10d
Differentiate \(h(t)=3t^2+2t+1,\ t\in\mathbb R\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(h\prime(t)=6t+2\)
  1. \((3t^2)\prime=6t\), \((2t)\prime=2\), constant 1 differentiates to 0.
10e
Differentiate \(h(t)=\sqrt[4]t-4e^{2t},\ t>0\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(h\prime(t)=\frac1{4t^{3/4}}-8e^{2t}\)
  1. \(\sqrt[4]t=t^{1/4}\); derivative is \(\tfrac14t^{-3/4}\).
  2. \((e^{2t})\prime=2e^{2t}\) by chain rule, retaining the coefficient −4.
10f
Differentiate \(f(x)=e^x+x^e,\ x>0\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=e^x+e x^{e-1}\)
  1. \(e\) is a fixed real exponent in \(x^e\); use the power rule.
10g
Differentiate \(f(x)=x^2\sin x\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=2x\sin x+x^2\cos x\)
  1. \((uv)\prime=u\prime v+uv\prime\) with \(u=x^2,\ v=\sin x\).
10h
Differentiate \(f(\theta)=\theta\cos\theta\sin\theta\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(\theta)=\sin\theta\cos\theta+\theta\cos 2\theta\)
  1. Differentiate three factors using product rule.
  2. \((\cos\theta\sin\theta)\prime=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta=\cos 2\theta\).
10i
Differentiate \(f(x)=\sin x+\cos x\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=\cos x-\sin x\)
  1. Differentiate the two trig terms separately; the derivative of cosine is negative sine.
10j
Differentiate \(f(\theta)=\cos(\theta^2)\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(\theta)=-2\theta\sin(\theta^2)\)
  1. Outer derivative: −sin(inner). Inner derivative: 2θ. Multiply.
10k
Differentiate \(f(x)=e^{x^2-x}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=(2x-1)e^{x^2-x}\)
  1. \(u=x^2-x\Rightarrow u\prime=2x-1\).
  2. \((e^u)\prime=e^u u\prime\).
10l
Differentiate \(f(t)=\sqrt{2t+1},\ t\ge-\frac12\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(t)=\frac1{\sqrt{2t+1}}\)
  1. \((\sqrt u)\prime=u\prime/(2\sqrt u)\) with \(u=2t+1,\ u\prime=2\).
  2. The displayed derivative is finite only for t>−1/2.
10m
Differentiate \(f(\theta)=\tan^2(n\theta),\ \theta\ne\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{2n}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(\theta)=2n\tan(n\theta)\sec^2(n\theta)\)
  1. Outer square → 2tan(inner); tan derivative → sec²; inner nθ → n.
  2. Assume n≠0 for the written exclusion formula; k,n integers.
10n
Differentiate \(y(t)=\ln|1+t-t^3|\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(y\prime(t)=\frac{1-3t^2}{1+t-t^3}\)
  1. \((\ln|u|)\prime=u\prime/u\) with \(u=1+t-t^3\).
  2. Important: the expression is defined only when 1+t−t³≠0; the printed exclusion t≠−1 alone is not its actual full domain.
10o
Differentiate \(f(x)=\log_{10}\sqrt x,\ x>0\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=\frac1{2x\ln10}\)
  1. \(\log_{10}\sqrt x=\ln x/(2\ln10)\).
  2. Differentiate ln x and retain the constant denominator.
10p
Differentiate \(f(x)=\ln(\cos x),\ \cos x>0\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=-\tan x\)
  1. \((\ln u)\prime=u\prime/u\) gives \(-\sin x/\cos x=-\tan x\).
10q
Differentiate \(f(x)=\ln(\sin^2x),\ \sin^2x>0\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=2\cot x\)
  1. \(u=\sin^2x\Rightarrow u\prime=2\sin x\cos x\).
  2. \(u\prime/u=2\cos x/\sin x=2\cot x\).
10r
Differentiate \(f(x)=\frac1{\ln x},\ x\in(0,1)\cup(1,\infty)\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=-\frac1{x(\ln x)^2}\)
  1. \(f=(\ln x)^{-1}\); outer derivative −(ln x)⁻² then multiply by 1/x.
10s
Differentiate \(f(x)=\tan^{-1}(x^2)\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=\frac{2x}{1+x^4}\)
  1. \((\arctan u)\prime=u\prime/(1+u^2)\) with \(u=x^2\).
10t
Differentiate \(f(x)=\sin^{-1}(2x+1)\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=\frac2{\sqrt{1-(2x+1)^2}}\)
  1. \((\arcsin u)\prime=u\prime/\sqrt{1-u^2}\) with \(u=2x+1\).
  2. Actual real domain is −1≤x≤0 (the handout prints [−1,1]); derivative exists for −1
10u
Differentiate \(f(x)=\arctan\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{1+x}},\ -1
Show worked solution+
Result \(f\prime(x)=-\frac1{2\sqrt{1-x^2}}\)
  1. Recognize \(\arctan\sqrt{(1-x)/(1+x)}=\tfrac12\arccos x\) for −1
  2. Differentiate the half-arccos identity; derivative requires −1
11

Implicit differentiation

Unknown y as a function of x
Source p.2
Lecture Differentiation slides 13–17Ref sheet A4 · Implicit derivativeRelated Tutorial 10g, 10k
Method Differentiate both sides → multiply derivative of y by y′ → collect y′.
11a
Differentiate implicitly: \(\frac{x^2}{x+y}=y^2+1\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x^2+2xy}{x^2+2y(x+y)^2}\)
  1. \(\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x^2}{x+y}=\frac{2x(x+y)-x^2(1+y\prime)}{(x+y)^2}\).
  2. \(2x(x+y)-x^2-x^2y\prime=2yy\prime(x+y)^2\).
  3. Collect the terms multiplying y′, then divide.
11b
Differentiate implicitly: \(y\cos x=x^2+y^2\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(y\prime=\frac{2x+y\sin x}{\cos x-2y}\)
  1. \(y\prime\cos x-y\sin x=2x+2yy\prime\) by product and chain rules.
  2. Bring terms in y′ together: \(y\prime(\cos x-2y)=2x+y\sin x\).
11c
Differentiate implicitly: \(e^{x/y}=x-y\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(y\prime=\frac{y e^{x/y}-y^2}{x e^{x/y}-y^2}\)
  1. \(e^{x/y}(y-xy\prime)/y^2=1-y\prime\).
  2. Multiply by y² and isolate y′. The expression is on points where y≠0 and resulting denominator≠0.
11d
Differentiate implicitly: \(xe^y=x-y\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(y\prime=\frac{1-e^y}{1+xe^y}\)
  1. \(e^y+xe^y y\prime=1-y\prime\).
  2. \(y\prime(xe^y+1)=1-e^y\).
12

Construct sketches from extrema

Absolute vs local extrema
Source p.2
Lecture Differentiation slides 18–22, 32–34Ref sheet A5/A9 · Extrema and sketchesRelated Tutorial 13, 14, 23
Method Build a continuous piecewise graph meeting all stated high/low points.
12a
Sketch a continuous function on \([1,5]\) with absolute max at 5, absolute min at 2, local max at 3, local min at 2.
Show worked solution+
Result \(\text{One valid continuous polygonal graph}\)
  1. Choose plotted coordinates \((1,1),(2,0),(3,2),(4,1),(5,3)\).
  2. Join them continuously: x=5 is highest, x=2 lowest, and x=3 is higher than its neighbors.
  3. Many different correct sketches exist.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
12b
Sketch a continuous function on \([1,5]\) with absolute min at 3, absolute max at 4, local max at 2.
Show worked solution+
Result \(\text{One valid continuous polygonal graph}\)
  1. Choose \((1,1),(2,2),(3,-1),(4,3),(5,1)\) and join continuously.
  2. At x=2 there is a local peak, x=3 is the global low and x=4 global high.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
13

Maximum attained, minimum not attained

Continuity and Extreme Value Theorem
Source p.2
Lecture Differentiation slides 18–20Ref sheet A5 · EVT conditionsRelated Tutorial 12, 14
Method A function on a closed interval need not have both extrema unless it is continuous.
13
Sketch a function on \([-1,2]\) with absolute maximum but no absolute minimum.
Show worked solution+
Result \(f(x)=\begin{cases}1&x=-1\\x+1&-1
  1. Take f(−1)=1 and f(x)=x+1 elsewhere in the interval.
  2. The infimum 0 is approached as x→−1⁺ but never reached; the absolute maximum is f(2)=3.
  3. Discontinuity at −1 is necessary here, since continuous functions on compact intervals attain both extrema.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
14

Local peak without an absolute maximum

Local extrema vs nonattained supremum
Source p.2
Lecture Differentiation slides 18–22Ref sheet A5 · EVT and local valuesRelated Tutorial 12, 13
Method Create a local hump, and an excluded limiting upper height larger than every attained height.
14
Sketch a function on \([-1,2]\) with a local maximum but no absolute maximum.
Show worked solution+
Result \(\text{One discontinuous piecewise function}\)
  1. Choose f(−1)=0; for −1
  2. For 0≤x≤2 choose f=1.2+1.2x−0.6x²; it has a local max at x=1 (height 1.8).
  3. Since values approach 2.8 at x→−1⁺ but never reach it, no absolute maximum occurs.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
15

Critical numbers

f′ zero or undefined, but x must lie in domain
Source p.2
Lecture Differentiation slides 18–22Ref sheet A5 · Critical valuesRelated Tutorial 16, 22
Method Differentiate → solve f′=0 → also check defined f with undefined derivative.
15a
Find critical numbers: \(f(x)=4+\tfrac13x-\tfrac12x^2\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(x=\tfrac13\)
  1. \(f'(x)=\tfrac13-x\); set to 0.
15b
Find critical numbers: \(f(x)=2x^3-3x^2-36x\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(x=-2,\;3\)
  1. \(f'(x)=6x^2-6x-36=6(x-3)(x+2)\); set factors to zero.
15c
Find critical numbers: \(f(t)=t^4+t^3+t^2+1\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(t=0\)
  1. \(f'(t)=t(4t^2+3t+2)\).
  2. The quadratic discriminant is 9−32<0, so it has no real zero.
15d
Find critical numbers: \(g(y)=\frac{y-1}{y^2-y+1}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(y=0,\;2\)
  1. \(g'(y)=y(2-y)/(y^2-y+1)^2\).
  2. The denominator never vanishes on ℝ; solve numerator =0.
16

Absolute maxima and minima on closed intervals

Closed interval method
Source p.2
Lecture Differentiation slides 18–22Ref sheet A5 · Closed interval methodRelated Tutorial 15, 21
Method Check every interior critical candidate and BOTH endpoints.
16a
Find absolute extrema: \(f(x)=12+4x-x^2\) on \([0,5]\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\max=16\ (x=2),\quad\min=7\ (x=5)\)
  1. \(f'(x)=4-2x=0\Rightarrow x=2\).
  2. \(f(0)=12,\ f(2)=16,\ f(5)=7\); compare.
16b
Find absolute extrema: \(f(x)=x+1/x\) on \([0.2,4]\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\max=\tfrac{26}5\ (x=\tfrac15),\quad\min=2\ (x=1)\)
  1. \(f'(x)=1-1/x^2=0\Rightarrow x=1\) inside the interval.
  2. \(f(1/5)=26/5,\ f(1)=2,\ f(4)=17/4\); compare.
16c
Find absolute extrema: \(f(t)=t-\sqrt[3]t\) on \([0,5]\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\max=5-\sqrt[3]5\ (t=5),\quad\min=-\tfrac2{3\sqrt3}\ (t=\tfrac1{3\sqrt3})\)
  1. \(f'(t)=1-\frac1{3t^{2/3}}\) for t>0, set to 0: \(t=1/(3\sqrt3)\).
  2. At t=0 derivative is undefined but f exists; include t=0 as the endpoint.
  3. \(f(0)=0,\ f(1/(3\sqrt3))=-2/(3\sqrt3),\ f(5)=5-\sqrt[3]5\); compare.
16d
Find absolute extrema: \(f(t)=\frac{\sqrt t}{1+t^2}\) on \([0,2]\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\max=\tfrac{3^{3/4}}4\ (t=1/\sqrt3),\quad\min=0\ (t=0)\)
  1. \(f'(t)=\frac{1-3t^2}{2\sqrt t(1+t^2)^2}\) for t>0.
  2. Set numerator to zero: t=1/√3 in interval.
  3. \(f(0)=0,\ f(2)=\sqrt2/5,\ f(1/\sqrt3)=3^{3/4}/4\).
17

Rolle’s theorem

Continuity + differentiability + equal endpoints
Source p.3
Lecture Differentiation slides 22–23Ref sheet A6 · Rolle/MVTRelated Tutorial 18, 19
Method Check all THREE hypotheses before solving f′(c)=0.
17a
Check Rolle for \(f(x)=2x^2-4x+5\) on \([-1,3]\) and find c.
Show worked solution+
Result \(c=1\)
  1. Polynomial ⇒ continuous and differentiable everywhere.
  2. \(f(-1)=11=f(3)\) so endpoint condition holds.
  3. \(f'(x)=4x-4=0\Rightarrow c=1\in(-1,3)\).
17b
Check Rolle for \(f(x)=x+1/x\) on \([1/2,2]\) and find c.
Show worked solution+
Result \(c=1\)
  1. Both endpoints positive, so f is continuous and differentiable throughout interval.
  2. \(f(1/2)=5/2=f(2)\).
  3. \(f'(x)=1-x^{-2}=0\Rightarrow x=1\in(1/2,2)\).
18

Why Rolle can fail

Cusp breaks differentiability
Source p.3
Lecture Differentiation slides 22–23Ref sheet A6 · Hypotheses firstRelated Tutorial 17, 20
Method One missing theorem condition means no guarantee.
18
For \(f(x)=1-x^{2/3}\), explain why \(f(1)=f(-1)\) but no interior c has \(f'(c)=0\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\text{Not differentiable at }x=0\)
  1. \(f(\pm1)=0\) for the real cube-root power.
  2. \(f'(x)=-\frac2{3\sqrt[3]x}\) for x≠0, never zero.
  3. At x=0 the derivative does not exist (sharp cusp), so Rolle’s differentiability hypothesis fails.
19

Mean Value Theorem

Secant slope equals a tangent slope
Source p.3
Lecture Differentiation slides 23–24Ref sheet A6 · Rolle/MVTRelated Tutorial 17, 20
Method Check hypotheses → average slope → solve f′(c)=average.
19a
Check MVT for \(f(x)=2x^2-3x+1\) on \([0,2]\) and find c.
Show worked solution+
Result \(c=1\)
  1. Polynomial is continuous [0,2] and differentiable (0,2).
  2. \([f(2)-f(0)]/2=(3-1)/2=1\).
  3. \(f'(x)=4x-3=1\Rightarrow c=1\).
19b
Check MVT for \(f(x)=\ln x\) on \([1,4]\) and find c.
Show worked solution+
Result \(c=\tfrac3{\ln4}\)
  1. ln x is continuous and differentiable on positive x.
  2. \([\ln4-\ln1]/3=\ln4/3\).
  3. \(1/c=\ln4/3\Rightarrow c=3/\ln4\in(1,4)\).
20

Failure of MVT at a discontinuity

Continuity requirement
Source p.3
Lecture Differentiation slides 23–24Ref sheet A6 · Rolle/MVTRelated Tutorial 18, 19
Method Investigate whether function is continuous on entire closed interval.
20
Show no \(c\in(1,4)\) satisfies \(f(4)-f(1)=f\prime(c)(4-1)\) for \(f(x)=(x-3)^{-2}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\text{MVT not applicable: discontinuous at }x=3\)
  1. \(f(1)=1/4,\ f(4)=1\) gives average slope \(1/4\).
  2. \(f'(x)=-2/(x-3)^3\); equation \(f'(c)=1/4\) gives \(c=1\), excluded endpoint.
  3. f undefined at x=3 in (1,4), violating continuity and differentiability hypotheses.
21

Increase, decrease, concavity, inflection

First/second derivative sign charts
Source p.3
Lecture Differentiation slides 24–28Ref sheet A7 · Sign chartsRelated Tutorial 22, 26
Method Find f′ sign → local extrema; f″ sign → concavity and inflections.
21a
Analyze \(f(x)=x^3-3x^2-9x+4\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\max_{\rm local}=9\ (x=-1),\ \min_{\rm local}=-23\ (x=3)\)
  1. \(f'=3(x-3)(x+1)\) ⇒ increasing \((-\infty,-1)\cup(3,\infty)\), decreasing \((-1,3)\).
  2. \(f(-1)=9,\ f(3)=-23\).
  3. \(f''=6x-6\) ⇒ concave down for x<1, up for x>1; inflection \((1,-7)\).
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
21b
Analyze \(f(x)=x/(x^2+1)\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\min_{\rm local}=-\tfrac12\ (x=-1),\ \max_{\rm local}=\tfrac12\ (x=1)\)
  1. \(f'=(1-x^2)/(x^2+1)^2\) ⇒ decreasing for |x|>1, increasing for |x|<1.
  2. \(f''=2x(x^2-3)/(x^2+1)^3\) changes sign at \(x=-\sqrt3,0,\sqrt3\).
  3. Concave down \((-\infty,-\sqrt3)\cup(0,\sqrt3)\); up \((-\sqrt3,0)\cup(\sqrt3,\infty)\). Inflection points \((-\sqrt3,-\sqrt3/4),(0,0),(\sqrt3,\sqrt3/4)\).
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
21c
Analyze \(f(x)=x^2-x-\ln x\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\min_{\rm local}=0\text{ at }x=1\)
  1. Domain x>0.
  2. \(f'=2x-1-1/x=\frac{(2x+1)(x-1)}x\) ⇒ decreasing (0,1), increasing (1,∞).
  3. \(f''=2+1/x^2>0\) for all x>0; concave up everywhere, no inflection.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
22

First and second derivative tests

Two ways to classify critical points
Source p.3
Lecture Differentiation slides 25–28Ref sheet A7 · Sign testsRelated Tutorial 15, 21
Method First derivative: sign switch. Second derivative: f″(c) positive/negative, after f′(c)=0.
22a
Use both tests for \(f(x)=1+3x^2-2x^3\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\text{local min }(0,1),\quad\text{local max }(1,2)\)
  1. \(f'=6x(1-x)=0\Rightarrow x=0,1\).
  2. First-test sign is −/+/− across 0,1: minimum then maximum.
  3. \(f''=6-12x\) gives \(f''(0)>0,\ f''(1)<0\); same result.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
22b
Use both tests for \(f(x)=x^2/(x-1),\ x\ne1\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\text{local max }(0,0),\quad\text{local min }(2,4)\)
  1. \(f'=x(x-2)/(x-1)^2\) zeros at 0 and 2; x=1 excluded, not a critical number.
  2. First-test signs +/− on either side of 0, and −/+ either side of 2.
  3. \(f''=2/(x-1)^3\) ⇒ negative at0 (max), positive at2 (min).
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
23

Sketch with signs of f′ and f″

Monotonicity and concavity
Source p.3
Lecture Differentiation slides 24–28, 32–34Ref sheet A7/A9 · ShapeRelated Tutorial 12, 26
Method Choose a function whose derivative and second derivative have the prescribed signs everywhere.
23a
Sketch any function with \(f'(x)<0\) and \(f''(x)<0\) for all real x.
Show worked solution+
Result \(f(x)=-e^x\)
  1. \(f=-e^x\Rightarrow f\prime=-e^x<0,\;f\prime\prime=-e^x<0\).
  2. Graph decreases while bending down, for all x.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
23b
Sketch any function with \(f'(x)>0\) and \(f''(x)>0\) for all real x.
Show worked solution+
Result \(f(x)=e^x\)
  1. \(f=e^x\Rightarrow f\prime=e^x>0,\;f\prime\prime=e^x>0\).
  2. Graph increases while bending up, for all x.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
24

Identify indeterminate forms

0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞−∞, 0⁰, 1^∞
Source p.4
Lecture Differentiation slides 28–32Ref sheet A8 · L’Hôpital/formsRelated Tutorial 25
Method Classify FORM before doing any differentiation; do not confuse an infinite result with indeterminacy.
24a
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(f/g\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(0/0\text{, indeterminate}\)
  1. Both numerator and denominator tend to zero; different rates can produce different answers.
24b
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(f/p\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(0\)
  1. Zero numerator over positive-infinite denominator tends to zero.
24c
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(h/p\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(0\)
  1. Finite numerator 1 over +∞ tends to zero.
24d
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(p/f\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\text{not indeterminate; sign-dependent unbounded}\)
  1. ∞/0 may be ±∞ or have different one-sided behavior; cannot assert one signed limit without more information.
24e
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(p/q\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\infty/\infty\text{, indeterminate}\)
  1. The relative growth of two divergent functions is unknown.
24f
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(p/h\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(+\infty\)
  1. The denominator tends to positive 1, so +∞/1 is +∞.
24g
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(fp\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(0\cdot\infty\text{, indeterminate}\)
  1. A vanishing factor times a diverging factor needs more rate information.
24h
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(h^p\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(1^\infty\text{, indeterminate}\)
  1. Base approaches 1 while exponent tends to infinity; use logarithms.
24i
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(f-p\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(-\infty\)
  1. Finite zero minus +∞ diverges negatively.
24j
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(p-q\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\infty-\infty\text{, indeterminate}\)
  1. Two divergent quantities could cancel, diverge or leave a finite difference.
24k
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(f^g\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(0^0\text{, indeterminate}\)
  1. Formal indeterminate-power label assumes the real powers are defined near the limit point (positive base).
24l
Given \(\lim f=0,\ \lim g=0,\ \lim h=1,\ \lim p=\infty,\ \lim q=\infty\) as \(x\to a\). Classify: \(h^f\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(1\)
  1. With positive base tending to 1 and exponent tending to 0, use exp(f ln h)→exp(0)=1.
25

Evaluate tricky limits

Factorization, L’Hôpital and logarithmic forms
Source p.4
Lecture Differentiation slides 28–32Ref sheet A8 · Limit diagnosisRelated Tutorial 24, 10
Method Substitute → classify → simplify or use L’Hôpital only in 0/0 or ∞/∞; take logs for powers.
25a
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to3}\frac{x-3}{x^2-9}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\frac16\)
  1. \((x^2-9)=(x-3)(x+3)\); cancel common factor for x≠3.
  2. \(1/(x+3)\to1/6\).
25b
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{2x}-1}{\sin x}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(2\)
  1. 0/0; apply L’Hôpital:
  2. \(\lim 2e^{2x}/\cos x=2\).
25c
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2}{1-\cos x}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(2\)
  1. 0/0; differentiate twice:
  2. \(\lim 2x/\sin x=\lim2/\cos x=2\).
25d
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{e^{x/10}}{x^3}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(+\infty\)
  1. ∞/∞; apply L’Hôpital three times, reaching a positive multiple of \(e^{x/10}\).
  2. An exponential eventually dominates every positive polynomial power.
25e
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{\ln\sqrt x}{x^2}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(0\)
  1. \(\ln\sqrt x=\tfrac12\ln x\).
  2. ∞/∞; L’Hôpital gives \((1/(2x))/(2x)=1/(4x^2)\to0\).
25f
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0^+}\frac{\ln x}{x}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(-\infty\)
  1. \(\ln x\to-\infty\) while \(x\to0^+\) is positive small.
  2. The quotient diverges to −∞, not an indeterminate form.
25g
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-1-x}{x^2}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\frac12\)
  1. 0/0; L’Hôpital once gives \((e^x-1)/(2x)\) (still 0/0).
  2. Differentiate again: \(e^x/2\to1/2\).
25h
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}\frac{9^x-2^x}{x}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\ln(9/2)\)
  1. 0/0, differentiate numerator:
  2. \(9^x\ln9-2^x\ln2\to\ln9-\ln2=\ln(9/2)\).
25i
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to\infty}(x-\ln x)\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(+\infty\)
  1. ∞−∞: compare rates with \(x(1-\ln x/x)\).
  2. \(\ln x/x\to0\) so the expression grows as x and tends to +∞.
25j
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to\infty}x\ln(1-1/x)\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(-1\)
  1. Transform product to quotient \(\ln(1-1/x)/(1/x)\) (0/0).
  2. L’Hôpital: \(\frac{(1/x^2)/(1-1/x)}{-1/x^2}\to-1\).
25k
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0^+}(1+\sin3x)^{1/x}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(e^3\)
  1. Form 1^∞. Let y denote expression, then \(\ln y=\ln(1+\sin3x)/x\).
  2. 0/0; L’Hôpital gives \(3\cos3x/(1+\sin3x)\to3\).
  3. \(y\to e^3\).
26

Full curve sketching

A–H graph investigation
Source p.4
Lecture Differentiation slides 32–34; derivative tests slides 24–28Ref sheet A9 · Curve sketch A–HRelated Tutorial 21, 22, 23
Method A domain → B intercepts → C symmetry → D asymptotes → E f′ → F extrema → G f″ → H plot.
26a
Sketch the curve \(y=\frac{2x^2}{x^2-1}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\text{even; vertical }x=\pm1,\;\text{horizontal }y=2\)
  1. A: Domain ℝ\\{−1,1}; B: only intercept (0,0); C: even about y-axis.
  2. D: x=−1,+1 are vertical asymptotes; y=2 horizontal as x→±∞.
  3. \(f'=-4x/(x^2-1)^2\) ⇒ increasing for x<0 within each branch; decreasing x>0; local max at (0,0).
  4. \(f''=4(3x^2+1)/(x^2-1)^3\) ⇒ down on (−1,1), up outside; no inflections within domain.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
26b
Sketch the curve \(y=\frac{x^2}{\sqrt x+1}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\text{domain }x\ge0,\;\text{increasing for }x>0\)
  1. A: Domain [0,∞); B: (0,0) only intercept; C: no even/odd symmetry.
  2. D: no vertical asymptote at 0; y→∞ as x→∞, no horizontal asymptote.
  3. \(f'=\frac{x(3\sqrt x+4)}{2(\sqrt x+1)^2}>0\) for x>0: increasing and no interior extremum.
  4. Second derivative is positive on x>0, so the curve bends upward. The one-sided endpoint minimum is (0,0).
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
26c
Sketch the curve \(f(x)=e^{2x}-e^x\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\min=(-\ln2,-\tfrac14),\ \text{inflection}=(-\ln4,-\tfrac3{16})\)
  1. Domain ℝ; intercept (0,0); x→−∞ gives horizontal asymptote y=0 from below.
  2. \(f'=e^x(2e^x-1)\) ⇒ decreases until x=−ln2, then increases; minimum (−ln2,−1/4).
  3. \(f''=e^x(4e^x-1)\) ⇒ inflection (−ln4,−3/16); bends down before and up afterward.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
26d
Sketch the curve \(f(x)=xe^x\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\min=(-1,-1/e),\ \text{inflection}=(-2,-2/e^2)\)
  1. Domain ℝ; x- and y-intercept (0,0); left-side horizontal asymptote y=0.
  2. \(f'=e^x(x+1)\) ⇒ decreasing (−∞,−1), increasing (−1,∞); min at (−1,−1/e).
  3. \(f''=e^x(x+2)\) ⇒ down for x<−2, up for x>−2; inflection (−2,−2/e²).
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
26e
Sketch the curve \(f(x)=\frac{\cos x}{2+\sin x}\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\text{period }2\pi,\ \min=-1/\sqrt3,\ \max=1/\sqrt3\)
  1. A: Domain ℝ (2+sin x≥1). B: zero where cos x=0; y-intercept 1/2; C: periodic 2π.
  2. \(f'=-(2\sin x+1)/(2+\sin x)^2\) ⇒ extrema when sin x=−1/2.
  3. Minimum at x=7π/6+2kπ with value −1/√3; maximum at x=11π/6+2kπ with value 1/√3.
  4. \(f''=-2\cos x(1-\sin x)/(2+\sin x)^3\); concavity changes where cos x=0, at x=π/2+kπ.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
26f
Sketch the curve \(f(x)=\ln(4-x^2)\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\max=(0,\ln4),\ \text{vertical }x=\pm2\)
  1. Domain −2
  2. As x→−2⁺ or 2⁻, ln(4−x²)→−∞, so x=±2 are vertical asymptotes.
  3. \(f'=-2x/(4-x^2)\) ⇒ increases on (−2,0), decreases on (0,2), max (0,ln4).
  4. \(f''=-2(4+x^2)/(4-x^2)^2<0\) throughout domain; no inflection.
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
26g
Sketch the curve \(f(x)=\frac1x+\ln x\).
Show worked solution+
Result \(\min=(1,1),\ \text{inflection }(2,\tfrac12+\ln2)\)
  1. Domain x>0; y-intercept none; no x-intercepts since the absolute minimum is 1.
  2. As x→0⁺, 1/x dominates ln x and f→∞. As x→∞, f→∞.
  3. \(f'=(x-1)/x^2\) ⇒ decreasing (0,1), increasing (1,∞), min (1,1).
  4. \(f''=(2-x)/x^3\) ⇒ concave up (0,2), down (2,∞), inflection (2,1/2+ln2).
Graph: shape and behavior (not a substitute for the algebra above)
